    3.1.5 What's Happening on the Network?

    1 of 2 activities complete
    Continue

    It starts like any normal morning: students log in, classes open websites, and devices send data across the network. Sometimes, attackers try to get in the way of that traffic, secretly watch it, redirect it, or overwhelm the network so normal users cannot get through.

    Open each card below. Make a prediction first, then run the attack and watch what happens to the traffic. Finish each card by deciding which parts of the CIA triad the attack threatens.

    ○Activity 1: Work through all four attack cards: predict, then make the CIA call

    Predict first. An attacker on the school Wi-Fi wants to read a student's traffic without the student noticing anything. Which device does the attacker need to pretend to be?

    Correct. Every device sends outside traffic to the gateway, so pretending to be the gateway puts the attacker in the path of everything. Now watch it happen.

    Every device on the network keeps a small table that pairs the gateway's IP address with a MAC address. If an attacker can convince the student's laptop that the attacker's MAC address belongs to the gateway, the laptop will hand its traffic to the attacker first. Run both versions below and watch where the login packet goes.

    Student Laptop
    Gateway
    Attacker

    What is happening

    1. Choose Normal day or Run the attack, then use Next step to follow the login packet at your own pace.

    Which parts of the CIA triad does this attack threaten? Select every one that applies, then check.

    This is ARP (Address Resolution Protocol) poisoning combined with MAC (Media Access Control) spoofing. The attacker sends fake ARP replies so every device records the attacker's MAC address as the gateway's. It works because ARP trusts any reply it receives and never checks who sent it.

    Predict first. A switch is the device that forwards traffic inside the local network. It remembers which MAC address is on which port so each packet goes only to the right device. What would an attacker have to do to see traffic that is not addressed to them?

    Correct. If the switch cannot remember where devices are, it stops delivering packets to one port and starts sending them everywhere. Now watch it happen.

    The switch's address table has limited space. An attacker can send thousands of packets from made-up MAC addresses until the table is full. Once the switch cannot learn where a device lives, it plays it safe and sends the packet out every port. The row of boxes on the switch is its address table. Watch it fill up as you run the attack.

    Student Laptop
    Attacker
    SwitchAddress table: 2 of 8 entries
    Teacher Laptop
    Printer

    What is happening

    1. Choose Normal day or Run the attack, then use Next step to follow the file at your own pace.

    Which parts of the CIA triad does this attack threaten? Select every one that applies, then check.

    This is MAC flooding combined with sniffing. The attacker fills the switch's address table with fake MAC addresses until it has no room to learn real ones. It works because a switch that cannot find a destination in its table falls back to sending the packet to every port, and sniffing means capturing and reading that traffic.

    Predict first. A student types the school portal's address into a browser. What actually decides which server the browser connects to?

    Not quite. Try a different option.

    Predict first. An attacker wants to knock the school's testing server offline but only has one laptop. How could a single laptop produce enough traffic to do that?

    Correct. One forged request can make dozens of devices reply to the server at the same time, multiplying the attacker's traffic. Now watch it happen.

    The attacker sends a request to the network's broadcast address, which every device answers. The trick is that the attacker forges the sender address so it looks like the request came from the testing server. Every device replies to the server instead of the attacker. Watch the server's load meter as the rounds pile up.

    Student
    Attacker
    Lab PC 1
    Lab PC 2
    Lab PC 3
    Lab PC 4
    Testing Server

    What is happening

    1. Choose Normal day or Run the attack, then use Next step to watch the load meter at your own pace.

    Which parts of the CIA triad does this attack threaten? Select every one that applies, then check.

    This is a smurf attack, one type of Denial of Service (DoS) attack. The attacker sends a broadcast request with the victim's address forged as the sender, so every device on the network replies to the victim at once. It works because one small forged packet triggers many replies, and the server cannot tell them apart from real requests.

    ✓Activity 2: Correctly identify all four attacks

    Identify the Attack

    Read what each person is saying and figure out what kind of attack they are describing. Look for the big clue: Was traffic intercepted, exposed, redirected, or was a service overwhelmed?

    1

    “Something is wrong with the device in the server closet. It started sending traffic out to every port instead of just the right ones. I'm worried that someone on the network may have been able to see traffic that wasn't meant for them.”

    IT Administrator

    Correct. This is known as MAC flooding and sniffing. MAC flooding overwhelmed the device's address table with fake entries. Once full, the device could not route traffic selectively and began broadcasting, which allowed an attacker to observe traffic not addressed to them.

    2

    “I logged into the school portal like normal this morning, but IT just called and said my account was used to access files I never touched. I typed my password into the site myself. How did anyone else get it?”

    Teacher, 3rd floor

    Correct. This is known as DNS poisoning and credential harvesting. The teacher was redirected to a fake version of the school portal through DNS poisoning. When they entered their credentials, the fake site collected them. That is the credential harvesting part of this attack.

    3

    “I was just browsing in the library and everything seemed fine, but the network admin flagged my laptop afterward. Apparently all my traffic was passing through some other device on the Wi-Fi before reaching the router. I didn't install anything.”

    Student, 2nd period

    Correct. This is known as ARP poisoning and MAC spoofing. An attacker used ARP poisoning to corrupt the local address table so the student's traffic was routed through the attacker's device first. MAC spoofing made that device appear to be the legitimate gateway.

    4

    “The testing platform went down right in the middle of state exams. Server logs are showing a huge spike in requests coming in from all over the place at the same time. We had to hand out paper tests. This feels coordinated.”

    IT Director

    Correct. This is known as a smurf attack / DoS. The testing platform was hit with a flood of traffic from many devices at once. The attacker's goal was not to steal data but to make the service unavailable at the worst possible moment.

    4 of 4 correct
